title: Muons that live too long
teaches: Why light's speed is the same for everyone, why that makes moving clocks run slow, and how muons raining down a mountain prove it

blocks.text: As you read this, something is passing through your hand about once a second. It came from the top of the atmosphere, and it is called a **muon**.

Space is full of fast particles, mostly protons flung out by exploding stars, which go by the misleading name of cosmic rays. When one of them hits a molecule of air, fifteen kilometres or so above your head, the collision makes a spray of new particles. Among them are muons: heavy cousins of the electron, which plunge on downwards at very nearly the speed of light. A muon is not built to last. Left to itself it falls apart, on average, in 2.2 millionths of a second.

Here is the trouble. Even at the speed of light, 300,000 kilometres a second, 2.2 millionths of a second gets you about 660 metres. A muon made fifteen kilometres up should be long gone before it gets anywhere near the ground. Yet they arrive in their thousands. Detectors in basements count them; they leave thin straight tracks in a cloud chamber, the misty box physicists use to see the paths of charged particles.

In 1963 two physicists at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, David Frisch and James Smith, did the sum properly. They hauled a muon counter up Mount Washington in New Hampshire, 1,907 metres above the sea, and counted about 560 muons an hour passing at the right speed. Then they took it down to Cambridge, at sea level, and counted again. If a muon's clock ticked like ours, only about thirty an hour should have survived the trip down. They counted about 410.

Either the muons were living longer, or something was wrong with the clocks. It is the clocks. To see why, you have to go back to a question about light that had been nagging physicists for forty years.

In 1865 the Scottish physicist James Clerk Maxwell wrote down the laws of electricity and magnetism in a few lines and found that they allowed a wave: a ripple of electric and magnetic push that would travel on its own. He worked out its speed from measurements anyone could make on a laboratory bench, with magnets and charged plates. It came out at almost exactly the speed of light, which Bradley's starlight (in *How far are the stars?*) had measured a century before.[^romer] Light, Maxwell said, is that wave.

It was a triumph with an awkward question in it. Every wave anyone knew was a wave *in* something. Sound is a wave in air; ripples are waves in water. So light must be a wave in some invisible stuff filling all of space, which physicists called the **ether**. And Maxwell's speed would then be its speed through the ether, just as the speed of sound is its speed through still air. The Earth swings round the Sun at 30 kilometres a second. It must be ploughing through the ether, and a beam of light sent upwind should go slightly slower, measured from the Earth, than one sent across.

In 1887, in Cleveland, Albert Michelson and Edward Morley built an instrument to catch that difference. It split a beam of light in two, sent the halves out at right angles and back, and laid them over each other, so that the slightest lag in one half would shift a pattern of light and dark stripes. To keep it still they built it on a slab of stone floating in a bath of mercury, and turned it slowly round. It could have caught an ether wind a hundred times weaker than the one they expected.

The stripes didn't move. They tried at different times of day and different seasons. Light went at the same speed in every direction, as if the Earth were standing still in the ether, which nobody believed. The Irish physicist George FitzGerald and the Dutchman Hendrik Lorentz suggested a patch: perhaps motion through the ether squeezes the instrument along its direction of travel, by exactly enough to hide the wind. It worked, and it looked like what it was, a patch.

In 1905 a twenty-six-year-old clerk at the patent office in Bern, Albert Einstein, published a paper that simply took the puzzle at its word. Suppose, he said, that light really does go at the same speed for everyone, whichever way they are moving, and that no experiment of any kind can tell you whether you are “really” moving or standing still. Then there is no need for an ether at all. (Einstein later said Michelson and Morley's result played little part in his own thinking; he got there by worrying about Maxwell's equations. But it was there, waiting, when he did.)

That sounds harmless. It isn't. If you are on a train doing 100 kilometres an hour and throw a ball forward at 20, someone on the platform sees it go at 120. Speeds add up. Einstein was saying that if you shine a torch forward from the train, the platform sees the light going at exactly the same speed as you do. Not light's speed plus the train's: the same. For both of you to be right about light, something else has to give. What gives is time.
Build the simplest clock there is: two mirrors, one above the other, and a pulse of light bouncing between them. Each trip up and down is one tick. Call it a **light clock**. Put one on a train.

blocks.caption: A light clock on a moving train. On the train the light goes straight up and down; from the platform the mirrors move on while it travels, so its path is a zigzag.
blocks.task: Make a prediction, then speed the train up to 87% of the speed of light

blocks.text: From the platform, the light has to go further between bounces, because the mirrors move on while it travels. If its speed is the same for the platform as for the train, a longer path takes longer, so each tick takes longer. The platform sees the train's clock run slow. At 87% of light's speed, it ticks at half the rate.

Nothing about this is special to light clocks. If the train's wristwatches, heartbeats and boiled eggs kept to a different time from its light clock, a passenger could tell they were moving by comparing them, and Einstein's starting point says no experiment can. So everything on the train runs slow, as seen from the platform. Here is the strangest part. The passengers see *the platform's* clocks running slow, by just the same amount, because from the train it is the platform that is moving. Both are right. Each person's own watch ticks perfectly normally; only the comparison between people moving past each other comes out different.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Light's speed is the same for everyone, so a clock moving past you ticks slower than yours, as you measure it. The faster it goes, the slower it ticks, and at the speed of light it would stop.
Nobody feels their own time slow down. It shows up only when clocks moving past each other are compared.

blocks.text: Now the muons. A muon falling down Mount Washington at 99.5% of light's speed is a clock moving very fast indeed. From the ground, its clock runs about ten times slow. The fall takes 6.4 millionths of a second by our watches, about three of a muon's lifetimes; but by the muon's own clock, only a tenth of that passes, and most of them make it.

blocks.caption: Muons falling from the summit of Mount Washington to the sea, 1,907 metres below: about 560 an hour at the top. Each line is a muon; a red dot marks where one decayed.
blocks.task: Make a prediction, then let moving clocks run slow and match Frisch and Smith's count

blocks.text: So what does the muon see? From where it sits, it is standing still and its clock is perfectly normal. It still lives 2.2 millionths of a second. But the mountain is rushing up at it at 99.5% of light's speed, and a moving thing is squashed along its direction of motion, by the same factor that slows its clocks. FitzGerald and Lorentz's patch turns out to be true, though not for their reason. To the muon the mountain is under two hundred metres high. It has plenty of time to cross that.

Two descriptions, one from the ground and one from the muon, and they agree on everything anyone can actually check: how many muons reach the counter at the bottom. The same result has been tested with clocks too. In 1971 two physicists flew atomic clocks round the world on ordinary airliners and found them out of step with the clocks they'd left behind, by the predicted few hundred billionths of a second.[^hafele]

This is Einstein's **special relativity**: “special” because it deals with the special case of steady motion, without gravity. The same theory, carried a step further, gives E = mc², the rule from *What makes the Sun shine?* that mass is a store of energy. Moving clocks and the Sun's fuel come from one idea.

parts.title: A map of place and time

blocks.text: If light's speed is the same for everyone, it is a limit. Push anything harder and harder and its clock slows, its mass-energy grows, and it gets closer and closer to light's speed without ever getting there. Nothing that carries a message travels faster.

That gives a picture which Stephen Hawking used more than any other. Draw a map with place across and time going up, scaled so that a flash of light runs at 45°. The flash from an event, here and now, spreads out into a cone: the **light cone**, everything the flash could reach. Anything you can ever affect lies inside the upper cone, because nothing goes faster than the flash. Anything that can have affected you lies inside the lower one. The rest, out to the sides, is too far away to reach in the time available: an exploding star a thousand light years away cannot have touched you yet, whatever it did.

blocks.caption: A light cone. Place runs across, time up, and a flash of light runs at 45°. A traveller's path, slower than light, always stays inside the cone.

blocks.text: Keep this picture. Gravity, it turns out, can tip light cones over, and that is how a black hole works (in *Dark stars*). And if you run the universe's light cones backwards, they all end on one point, which is the question at the end of the trunk, *Did time have a beginning?*

blocks.caption: Six questions on light, clocks and muons
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: A muon falling at nearly light speed lives long enough to reach the ground. Seen from the ground, why?
choices: Its clock runs slow, so it ages less on the way down
It is going faster than light
Muons live longer in air than in a vacuum
items.why: From the ground the muon is a fast-moving clock, running about ten times slow, so far fewer of its lifetimes pass during the fall.

items.ask: And seen by the muon itself?
choices: Its clock is normal, but the mountain is squashed to a fraction of its height
The ground is coming up at faster than light
items.why: To the muon it is at rest and its clock is normal. The mountain is moving, and moving things are shortened along their motion, by the same factor.

items.ask: Michelson and Morley expected light to go slower against the Earth's motion. What did they find?
choices: The same speed in every direction
A small difference, less than expected
A difference that changed with the seasons
items.why: No ether wind at all, at any time of day or year. Einstein's answer was that light's speed is the same for everyone.

items.ask: An astronaut flies past the Earth at 87% of light's speed. What does she notice about her own watch?
items.why: Each person's own clocks behave normally. Only when her watch is compared with Earth's clocks does the difference show, and she sees the Earth's clocks running slow.

items.ask: On a light-cone map, an event lies outside your cone, out to the side. What does that mean?
choices: Nothing you do now can affect it, and it can't affect you now
items.why: It is too far away for even light to reach in the time between. It is in neither your reachable future nor your past.

items.ask: How is special relativity connected to the Sun's shining?
choices: The same theory gives E = mc², the rule that turns lost mass into the Sun's energy
It isn't: one is about clocks, the other about heat
The Sun's light is slowed by relativity
items.why: E = mc² comes out of Einstein's 1905 theory. The mass lost when hydrogen fuses into helium becomes the Sun's light.

summary: **Muons should not reach the ground.** They live 2.2 millionths of a second, about 660 metres at light speed, yet they rain down from 15 km up.
**Light was thought to wave in an ether.** Maxwell showed light is an electric and magnetic wave; Michelson and Morley found no ether wind in 1887.
**Light's speed is the same for everyone.** Einstein, 1905: no experiment can tell who is really moving.
**Moving clocks run slow.** A light clock passing you ticks slower, as you measure it: half speed at 87% of light's speed. Your own watch always ticks normally.
**Two views, one answer.** From the ground the muon's clock is slow; from the muon the mountain is squashed. Frisch and Smith's count fits both.
**Nothing outruns light.** The light cone maps everything you can affect and everything that can affect you.
**This is special relativity.** The same theory gives E = mc².

hafele.title: Clocks on airliners
hafele.text: In October 1971 Joseph Hafele and Richard Keating bought round-the-world seats on scheduled flights, one trip eastward and one westward, for themselves and four atomic clocks (the clocks had their own tickets, under the name “Mr Clock”). Back at the Naval Observatory in Washington, the eastward clocks had lost about 59 billionths of a second against the ones left behind and the westward clocks had gained about 273. Both speed and height played a part: height, because clocks higher above the Earth run faster, which is the subject of *The Sun bends starlight*.

romer.title: Rømer's late moons
romer.text: The first sign that light takes time came in 1676, when the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer noticed that Jupiter's moon Io slipped into Jupiter's shadow later than predicted when Jupiter was far from the Earth, and earlier when it was near. The difference, he said, was the time light took to cross the extra distance: about twenty minutes across the Earth's orbit (the modern value is about sixteen and a half).
